props.title: Fighting
props.initialSlug: Small-town boxer joins NYC's underground scene

sections.content: Fighting (2009) sits at the intersection of bare-knuckle brawling films and New York City street hustler stories. Director Dito Montiel follows up his gritty A Guide to Recognizing Your Saints (2006) with this tale of underground fighting that echoes earlier classics like Hard Times (1975) and Bloodsport (1988). Channing Tatum's performance as Shawn MacArthur showcases his physical prowess while establishing the everyman charm that would later define his career. The film's raw fight sequences and authentic NYC locations capture the desperation of street-level hustling.

sections.content: The underground fighting genre peaked in the late 1980s with films like Kickboxer (1989) and Best of the Best (1989), where martial arts spectacle took center stage. Fighting marked a grittier turn, emphasizing economic desperation over tournament glory. This shift influenced later films like Warrior (2011) and Here Comes the Boom (2012), which grounded their combat in personal struggle rather than pure sport.

Terrence Howard's performance as hustler Harvey Boarden connects Fighting to a lineage of NYC street films including Mean Streets (1973) and American Gangster (2007). The film's focus on small-time operators rather than major criminals creates an intimate portrait of survival in the city's margins, similar to the approach in Before the Devil Knows You're Dead (2007). sections.content: The late 2000s saw combat sports films shift from traditional martial arts to mixed martial arts, reflecting the rising popularity of UFC. Fighting bridges this transition, incorporating street fighting elements while maintaining classical one-on-one showdowns. Later films like Warrior (2011) and Here Comes the Boom (2012) would fully embrace MMA aesthetics, while maintaining the personal drama that made Fighting compelling.
